name: United Republic of Tanzania
law:
▸WHAT THE LAW HERE COUNTS AS ENGINEERED
This country is not classified on the regime layer. That is a gap in this map rather than a finding about the country — almost every state has a biosafety law of some kind, and this one has not been read.
▸DECISIONS FILED TO THE CARTAGENA PROTOCOL
Nothing filed here has been harvested. The Clearing-House holds decisions from far more countries than this map has fetched, so an empty line is this map’s reach and not the country’s record.
Neither the GMO-free register nor the cultivation report names a region in this country. Neither source covers the whole world, so this is silence in the records rather than an absence on the ground.
act:
What you can do about this
▸TEST IT YOURSELF5
EnviroLogix QuickStix
TESTING
Lateral flow strips, the same format as a pregnancy test. Crush tissue or seed in water, dip, read in five to ten minutes. Sold to anyone, a few pounds each, in packs. Strips are trait-specific, so know which trait to look for before buying.
Visit source ↗
Romer Labs AgraStrip
TESTING
Strips plus the extraction kits that go with them, sold internationally — which matters because the trait to test for differs by region.
Visit source ↗
Agdia ImmunoStrip
TESTING
Sells in small quantities with published prices, which makes it the most usable of the three for someone testing a handful of samples rather than a lorry.
Visit source ↗
Eurofins — laboratory GMO testing
TESTING
The largest food and feed testing network in the world, with laboratories in more than 60 countries and the default commercial route for a confirmatory DNA test. A strip result tells you what to do next; this is what an enforcement body acts on.
Visit source ↗
GMOMETHODS — the EU database of validated detection methods, and the ENGL laboratory network
IF YOU ARE COMMISSIONING A TEST, THIS IS WHERE THE METHOD COMES FROM. An application to authorise a GM food or feed in the EU MUST INCLUDE A METHOD FOR DETECTING, IDENTIFYING AND QUANTIFYING IT, and the EU Reference Laboratory (EURL GMFF, hosted by the Joint Research Centre) validates that method for sensitivity, specificity, accuracy and reliability. The validated methods are then PUBLISHED FREE in the GMOMETHODS database, searchable by EVENT, UNIQUE IDENTIFIER, SPECIES, APPLICANT and technique. So for most authorised events anywhere in the world there is a published, peer-validated PCR method a laboratory can be asked to run — and the unique identifier this map keeps telling readers to write down is the key to finding it. The JRC also publishes decision tools, GMO-MATRIX and EVENT-FINDER. Behind it sits the EUROPEAN NETWORK OF GMO LABORATORIES (ENGL), the national enforcement laboratories of every EU country PLUS NORWAY, SWITZERLAND AND TURKEY. THE HONEST LIMIT: detecting UNAUTHORISED GMOs relies on screening that only indicates presence and needs confirmation by other approaches; and the EURL and ENGL's own report of 26 March 2019 addresses the difficulty of detecting organisms made by NEW MUTAGENESIS TECHNIQUES — gene-edited plants may leave nothing a method can target. Work on GM animals and microorganisms is still in progress.
Visit source ↗
▸WHO AUTHORISES A RELEASE3
National Environment Management Council
REGULATOR
Authorises. Tanzania halted its trials in 2018 and ordered material destroyed, having previously operated a strict liability rule that made researchers personally liable for any damage — which is why almost nobody applied. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.
Visit source ↗
Biosafety Clearing-House — national focal points
REGULATOR
Every party to the Cartagena Protocol must name a contact for biosafety, and the list is public. For most of the world it is the only named biosafety contact that exists, and it holds the decisions filed for that country.
Visit source ↗
Biosafety Clearing-House — what a country profile holds
Referenced by 135 rows in this box. A country profile on the Clearing-House holds the national focal point and competent authorities the country has notified, its national biosafety law where filed, and the decisions it has submitted under Article 20. It is a country's OWN FILINGS, so a thin profile means the country has filed little — not that it decides little. Filing is a treaty obligation without a sanction for missing it.
Visit source ↗
▸WHO TAKES A COMPLAINT7
TPHPA — Tanzania Plant Health and Pesticides Authority
COMPLAINT
Inspects and enforces. One caution about this source: the IPPC contact record is updated by the country itself and can lag — records checked here carried ministry names that had since changed. The named person, address and telephone are the useful part; treat the institutional name as a starting point and check it against the ministry's own site. Established by the PLANT HEALTH ACT No. 4 of 2020, which repealed the Plant Protection Act 1998, merging the ministry's Plant Health Services with the Tropical Pesticides Research Institute into a single authority and making it Tanzania's national plant protection organisation. Powers a reader can use: it registers pesticides and gazettes the list, and where a REGISTERED pesticide has been shown to damage human health, animal health or the environment the Registrar may, on the Authority's recommendation, TEMPORARILY PROHIBIT its import, sale, distribution and use. It can re-evaluate a registration on reasonable grounds, and the Act covers substandard, counterfeit and adulterated pesticides, compensation for damage or loss suffered, and post-entry quarantine. Note a conflict-of-interest rule: board members, staff and agents may not trade in pesticides or regulated articles during their term or for one year after. Headquarters Ngaramtoni, Arusha; the old tpri.go.tz still resolves. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.
Tanzania Bureau of Standards
COMPLAINT
Handles food labelling standards and complaints. Established 1975 under the industry and trade ministry, with regional offices in Dodoma, Mwanza, Arusha, Mbeya and Mtwara as well as Dar es Salaam. Two things make it the practical route here. It is Tanzania's National Enquiry Point for the WTO technical barriers and sanitary and phytosanitary agreements, so it holds the technical regulations and proposed standards a reader would otherwise have to find country by country. And it runs product and premise registration and food risk assessment, which means it is the body a sample and a complaint both reach. IT DOES ENFORCE, and it gained the power recently. From 1 July 2019 the Finance Act amended the Standards Act No. 2 of 2009 and moved food and cosmetics regulation from the Tanzania Food and Drugs Authority to TBS — TFDA keeping medicines and devices and renaming itself the Tanzania Medicines and Medical Devices Authority. So anything citing TFDA for a food question predates July 2019. Under the amended Act NO PERSON MAY MANUFACTURE, IMPORT, DISTRIBUTE, SELL OR EXPOSE FOR SALE pre-packaged food unless the product is registered by the Bureau, and TBS registers production premises as well. Imports run through Pre-shipment Verification of Conformity under section 4(1)(s): consignments without a certificate of conformity are rejected or fined at the port. One caveat from a 2025 sector review: the amendment did not tidy the other food safety laws, so overlaps with TMDA persisted until a memorandum of understanding separated them. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.
Visit source ↗
The Cartagena focal point, when nothing else is named
Every party to the Cartagena Protocol names a national focal point, and the Clearing-House publishes the current office. Where this map does not name the body that takes a complaint in a country, that office is the one obliged to answer a question about a living modified organism, and it can say which national authority handles the rest. It is the fallback of last resort rather than the right first stop: a focal point is a correspondence address, not an inspectorate.
Visit source ↗
IPPC national plant protection organisation contacts
Every IPPC contracting party maintains a national plant protection organisation, and its contact details are published country by country. This is the body that handles a plant pest or a quarantine question, and in most countries it is also the body with inspectors who can actually enter a field. Where a national complaint row here is empty, this is usually the office it would have named. Two limits, both found repeatedly while checking the rows that link here: the record is updated BY THE COUNTRY, so institutional names lag — several checked in this file named ministries and departments that had since merged, been renamed or been replaced — and the convention covers PLANT HEALTH, so a food-on-the-shelf or an animal question belongs elsewhere. Treat the named person and the telephone number as the useful part.
Visit source ↗
Codex Alimentarius contact points
Each Codex member names a national contact point for food standards. It does not take complaints itself, but it is the office that knows which national food authority does — useful in a country whose food safety functions are split across several ministries, which is most of them.
Visit source ↗
Consumers International — member organisations by country
The worldwide federation of consumer organisations, with a searchable member list by country. Worth knowing as a route because a consumer organisation can do two things a state inspectorate often will not: commission an independent laboratory test on a product it has simply bought, and publish the result. Tunisia's Institut National de la Consommation runs comparative tests on request through accredited laboratories and publishes them; several members elsewhere do the same. Where this map names no national complaint route, a member organisation is often the shortest path to a test somebody else pays for. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.
Rotterdam Convention — designated national authorities for pesticides
Every party to the Rotterdam Convention names a Designated National Authority for pesticides, and the register of them is public. It is worth knowing because it is a different lever from a complaint: the convention operates PRIOR INFORMED CONSENT on listed hazardous chemicals in international trade, so the DNA is the office through which a country can refuse import of a listed pesticide, and through which other countries are told of that refusal. In several states the DNA is the same person as the head of the plant protection organisation — in Nepal it is the chief of the Plant Quarantine and Pesticide Management Centre — so this can also be the fastest way to find who really holds pesticide policy.
Visit source ↗
▸WHERE AN APPLICATION IS ANNOUNCED5
Tanzania Government Gazette
CONSULTATION
Where the biosafety regulations and the strict liability rule were published. Not linked here: check for a current online edition, or ask the Cartagena focal point for the issue. The gazette is authoritative in print, and in most jurisdictions a measure takes effect on the date it is published there. Not linked here: check for a current online edition, or ask the Cartagena focal point for the issue.
Biosafety Clearing-House — decisions and consultations
CONSULTATION
Parties file their decisions here, and for most first imports for release a public consultation is required beforehand. For countries with no notice venue of their own, this is the only place an application becomes visible in advance.
Visit source ↗
European Forum of Official Gazettes
Where a gazette is the announcement venue, this forum lists the official journals of the EU and EFTA states with links to their online editions. It does not cover the rest of the world, and for most of the gazette rows on this map the print edition remains authoritative.
Visit source ↗
Cartagena Clearing-House — the decision even when the gazette is not online
A gazette is authoritative and often unreachable: Ethiopia's is sold in Addis Ababa, Namibia's has no online archive. But a party to the Cartagena Protocol files its decisions to the Clearing-House regardless, so the substance of what was authorised is usually readable there even where the official announcement is not. The date of gazette publication still governs when a measure takes effect.
Visit source ↗
Finding your country's official gazette — Guide to Law Online and the Michigan gazettes directory
THE FILE'S EXISTING GAZETTE ROW COVERS THE EU AND EFTA ONLY; this is the route everywhere else. In most countries A LAW ENTERS INTO FORCE ON THE DATE OF PUBLICATION IN THE OFFICIAL GAZETTE, and in civil law jurisdictions the gazette is often the SOLE SOURCE of the authoritative text until codes are updated — which is why an authorisation, a ban or a quarantine order may exist nowhere else. Two free directories find it: the LAW LIBRARY OF CONGRESS GUIDE TO LAW ONLINE, which lists legal resources online for every country with gazette details under the Legislative and Legal Guides sections; and GOVERNMENT GAZETTES ONLINE, a University of Michigan project giving DIRECT LINKS plus the language, publication frequency, time coverage and content of each — covering around sixty countries including Algeria, Burkina Faso, Congo, Djibouti, Kenya, Saint Lucia, Sri Lanka and Uruguay. For machine translation of texts in other languages, GLOBAL REGULATION. TWO LIMITS: the Library of Congress FOREIGN OFFICIAL GAZETTES (FOG) database IS NO LONGER UPDATED, and its own Foreign Legal Gazettes Guide covered only about HALF of the 240 jurisdictions it collects for as of early 2024. Where a gazette is unreachable, the Cartagena Clearing-House row in this box is the fallback.
Visit source ↗
▸WHO CERTIFIES, AND WHAT A POSITIVE TEST COSTS6
TOAM
CERTIFIER
The Tanzanian organic movement; certification runs through the East African mark.
Visit source ↗
IFOAM — Organics International
CERTIFIER
The global umbrella for organic standards, which exclude engineered material by definition in every member scheme. Use it to find the certifier operating where you are: a positive test costs an operator the certification and the price premium immediately, without a hearing.
Visit source ↗
Demeter International
CERTIFIER
Certifies biodynamic production in more than 60 countries to a standard stricter than organic, including on seed: varieties bred by methods it rejects cannot be used at all. Where no national organic body exists, an international certifier still operates.
Visit source ↗
IOAS — accreditation of organic certifiers
A certifier's own website will always say it is accredited; only the accreditor's register says whether that is still true. IOAS publishes the organic certification bodies it accredits, worldwide. Check a certificate against this before relying on it, and note that the EU, the US and several other jurisdictions run their own control-body lists as well — a body may be on one and not another. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.
Visit source ↗
EU list of recognised control bodies for organic imports
The Commission publishes the control bodies and control authorities recognised for organic production in third countries, each with a code of the form XX-BIO-NNN that appears on the product label. If a label carries such a code, this is where to check the body behind it is still listed — recognition has been withdrawn before, most visibly over fraudulent certification of raw Indian cotton. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.
Visit source ↗
PGS global map — participatory guarantee systems
Where a country's organic certification runs through participatory guarantee rather than a third-party auditor, this is where to find it: an IFOAM and FAO register searchable by country and product. It matters for this map because a PGS sets its own standard through its members, so what 'organic' excludes in a given initiative is decided locally rather than by a national regulation.
Visit source ↗
▸LEGAL HELP, IN THIS FIELD SPECIFICALLY9
TABIO — Tanzania Alliance for Biodiversity
LEGAL
Documented the strict liability regime and the 2018 halt to trials. Formed November 2011 as an ALLIANCE of civil society and private sector organisations rather than a single NGO, so it can convene where one body cannot. Its stated aims are conserving AGRO-BIODIVERSITY, promoting FARMERS' SELF-DETERMINATION AND FOOD SOVEREIGNTY, and facilitating exchange of information and experience between members. It works with partners across East Africa, so a Tanzanian question can be carried regionally. Read it with this country's other entries: TBS gained food regulation from TFDA in 2019 and TPHPA was created by the Plant Health Act 2020 — both recent, which makes an organised civil-society counterpart more useful than usual.
Visit source ↗
La Vía Campesina
LEGAL
The largest farmers' organisation in the world, 200 million smallholders across 81 countries, and the origin of the term food sovereignty. It supports members facing seed law and land disputes and has regional secretariats on every inhabited continent, so there is one within reach almost anywhere.
Visit source ↗
GRAIN
LEGAL
Researches and publishes on seed laws, land deals and corporate concentration, and works with local organisations rather than in one jurisdiction. Its published analysis of a country's seed law is often the only independent account of it in any language a reader here can use.
Visit source ↗
Third World Network — biosafety programme
LEGAL
Follows the Cartagena Protocol negotiations and publishes briefings for delegations from developing countries. Where a national law was drafted from a template, this is usually where the counter-analysis of that template was written.
Visit source ↗
Environmental Law Alliance Worldwide (ELAW)
LEGAL
Connects environmental lawyers in more than 70 countries and supplies scientific and legal support to local counsel free of charge. It is the practical answer for someone with a case and no lawyer who knows this subject: the local lawyer exists, and ELAW is what backs them.
Visit source ↗
Access Initiative — finding your rights to information and participation
LEGAL
Documents, country by country, what rights of access to environmental information, participation and justice actually exist in law. Worth reading before writing anything, because the answer differs enormously and is rarely obvious.
Visit source ↗
ITPGRFA — the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture
The treaty that recognises FARMERS' RIGHTS — Article 9 — including the protection of traditional knowledge, the right to participate in benefit-sharing from plant genetic resources, and the right to participate in national decisions about their use. It also states that nothing in the article limits farmers' rights to save, use, exchange and sell farm-saved seed, subject to national law. Each party names a national focal point, listed here. Two limits worth knowing: implementation is left to national law, so what Article 9 means in practice is decided domestically; and the treaty's multilateral system covers a listed set of crops rather than everything. Useful where a seed-law or variety-rights argument needs an international peg. LINK CHECKED AND FOUND DEAD: the page or host no longer answers. The body may well still exist — government sites move and rename constantly — so confirm through the worldwide routes in this box, or the Biosafety Clearing-House or IPPC contact page for this country, rather than treating the absence as evidence the body has gone.
Stockholm Convention — persistent organic pollutants, national focal points
Parties designate a national focal point and an official contact point, both listed here, and each prepares a National Implementation Plan setting out how it will eliminate or restrict the listed chemicals. Several of the pesticides this map's contamination records involve are listed under it. Where a national pesticide register is thin or unpublished, a country's implementation plan is often the fuller public document, and it is filed with the convention rather than with the ministry.
Visit source ↗
UNDROP — UN Declaration on the Rights of Peasants and Other People Working in Rural Areas
Adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2018 and named by only one row in this file until now, though it is the instrument several of the organisations here actually use. It recognises peasants' RIGHT TO SEEDS — including the right to save, use, exchange and sell farm-saved seed, to keep traditional knowledge, to participate in decisions on plant genetic resources, and to protection against loss of that knowledge — alongside rights to land, water and a healthy environment, and the right to PARTICIPATE IN DECISION-MAKING on matters affecting them. Two things to know before relying on it: it is a DECLARATION, not a treaty, so it binds nobody directly and works through domestic adoption and argument; and the OHCHR collects submissions on its implementation, which means a national account of how a government is or is not honouring it can be filed and read. Cameroon's RADD has used it that way — see this file's Cameroon entry.
Visit source ↗
▸LOOK UP A CLINIC, A LAB OR A TRIAL4
WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform
RECORDS
Searches every national trial register at once, so a gene or cell therapy trial registered in one country is findable from another. For a patient, this is where to check whether a treatment being offered is a registered trial at all — an unregistered one is a warning in itself.
Visit source ↗
ClinicalTrials.gov — tracing a sponsor
RECORDS
The largest single register, and it carries results as well as protocols. Search by condition and by intervention; the sponsor field is what ties a trial to the company entries on this map.
Visit source ↗
Global BioLabs — maximum-containment laboratories
RECORDS
No government publishes a register of high-containment laboratories. This research project is the only global account of where they are, and the source of the 118 on this map — including the ones still under construction, which is when a community can still ask about them.
Visit source ↗
Tracing the company behind a trial, a facility or a release — OpenCorporates and the GLEIF LEI
A SPONSOR NAME ON A TRIAL, AN APPLICANT ON A RELEASE PERMIT OR AN OPERATOR OF A FACILITY IS OFTEN A SUBSIDIARY, and this map's industry entries are only useful if the parent can be found. OPENCORPORATES draws from NATIONAL BUSINESS REGISTRIES IN AROUND 145 JURISDICTIONS — over 220 million companies and 300 million officers, PROVENANCED TO THE OFFICIAL SOURCE — giving current status, NAMED DIRECTORS and industry codes. GLEIF's LEGAL ENTITY IDENTIFIER database is the complement and is FREE: its LEVEL 2 DATA answers WHO OWNS WHOM, publishing the LEI of an entity's DIRECT AND ULTIMATE PARENT alongside the child record, and the reverse. The two are mapped to each other, and an LEI record also carries the HOME-REGISTRY NUMBER AND REGISTERING AUTHORITY, which is what lets you cross to the national register itself. TWO LIMITS: only entities that have obtained an LEI appear in the ownership layer, and a child may report an EXCEPTION where it has no parent, opts out for exceptional reasons, or its parents hold no LEI — so an absent parent is not proof of independence. Just over half the global LEI population is linked to OpenCorporates.
Visit source ↗
▸USE A TREATY RIGHT4
Aarhus Convention Compliance Committee
TREATY
Any member of the public may bring a communication against a party government — no fee, no lawyer, no nationality test, and no need to have exhausted the courts first in every case. It examines whether a state gave the public information, participation and access to justice on environmental decisions, which is exactly what a refused consultation is. It moves slowly, it works in public, and governments would rather it did not exist. 47 parties, mostly Europe and Central Asia.
Visit source ↗
Escazú Agreement — Latin America and the Caribbean
TREATY
The regional counterpart to Aarhus, and the only environmental treaty anywhere with an article obliging states to protect environmental defenders. It guarantees access to environmental information and participation in decisions, which reaches biosafety decisions directly.
Visit source ↗
Cartagena Protocol Article 23 — the right to be consulted
TREATY
Every party must consult the public on decisions about living modified organisms and make the results available. Where a country runs no consultation at all, this is the obligation it is not meeting — and citing it by article, in writing, is more use than an objection with no footing.
Visit source ↗
Nagoya–Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol — who pays
TREATY
Sets out response measures where a living modified organism causes damage to biodiversity. Ask in writing which provision applies and who would pay; the answer, or its absence, is the useful document. Only about 55 countries have ratified, so whether it applies where you are is itself worth establishing.
Visit source ↗
▸INSPECTION REPORTS AND WELFARE COMPLAINTS3
Animal welfare inspection — the general route
ANIMALS
Most countries license animal research through an agriculture, health or home affairs ministry and inspect on a schedule. Whether the public may complain, and whether reports are published, varies enormously — the two questions worth asking first.
The Animal Welfare Body inside the institution, and the WOAH animal welfare focal point
Two routes exist almost everywhere even where no public register does. FIRST, INSIDE THE INSTITUTION. Under EU DIRECTIVE 2010/63/EU — followed closely in Switzerland, the UK and Norway too — every authorised establishment MUST HAVE AN ANIMAL WELFARE BODY, comprising at least one person with practical knowledge of animal care and husbandry, ONE SCIENTIFIC MEMBER, AND A DESIGNATED VETERINARIAN. It advises on acquisition, care, housing and use, applies the 3Rs, KEEPS TRACK OF HOW PROJECTS AFFECT THE ANIMALS, and advises on project applications — so an internal record exists of what is being done and at what severity, and a NON-TECHNICAL PROJECT SUMMARY is published for each authorised project. National competent authorities grant authorisation and INSPECT breeders, suppliers and research establishments, and each Member State has a NATIONAL COMMITTEE for the protection of animals used for scientific purposes. SECOND, INTERNATIONALLY. Each of WOAH's 182 member countries nominates a NATIONAL FOCAL POINT FOR ANIMAL WELFARE, alongside focal points for veterinary laboratories and wildlife. Where no national body is named in this box, that focal point is a real named official who can be asked who licenses and who inspects. Note WOAH's animal welfare standards, unlike its health standards, DO NOT FALL UNDER THE WTO SPS AGREEMENT, so they carry no trade enforcement.
Visit source ↗
AAALAC International — the accredited-organisations directory, and what accreditation is and is not
WHERE NO GOVERNMENT PUBLISHES A LIST OF ANIMAL FACILITIES, THIS ONE IS PUBLIC AND SEARCHABLE. AAALAC International, a private non-profit founded 1965, PUBLISHES ITS FULL DIRECTORY OF ACCREDITED ORGANISATIONS BY NAME AND CITY — more than 1,140 institutions and companies in 52 countries, updated continuously, and it is the source of the animal-facility markers on this map. The process is substantive: the institution writes a PROGRAM DESCRIPTION covering policies, housing, veterinary care and facilities; AAALAC's Council on Accreditation reviews it and conducts an ON-SITE ASSESSMENT; deficiencies must be corrected within a set period. Accredited institutions must PROMPTLY REPORT ADVERSE EVENTS, INCLUDING UNEXPECTED ANIMAL DEATHS AND ALLEGATIONS OF COMPROMISED WELFARE; AAALAC investigates and can require corrective action or REVOKE ACCREDITATION. So an allegation can be made to the accreditor as well as to the regulator. THE LIMITS MATTER AS MUCH: accreditation is VOLUNTARY and private, so absence from the directory means nothing about whether a facility exists; the directory shows who holds it, not what was found; and AAALAC itself warns that institutions sometimes CLAIM ACCREDITATION THEY DO NOT HOLD — which is precisely why the directory is worth checking against a claim.
Visit source ↗
▸WHAT IS PUBLISHED, AND WHAT IS NOT1
Where the numbers come from, and what they leave out — CCAC, the UK count, and the countries with none
ONLY A HANDFUL OF COUNTRIES COUNT AT ALL, and each counts something different — which is why global totals in this field should be read as estimates. CANADA'S CCAC publishes an annual ANIMAL DATA REPORT with DOWNLOADABLE SORTABLE SPREADSHEETS breaking down species, purpose and INVASIVENESS CATEGORY — the most usable open dataset of its kind. BRITAIN counts every regulated procedure on a protected animal under the ANIMALS (SCIENTIFIC PROCEDURES) ACT 1986, covering all vertebrates AND CEPHALOPODS, published annually by the Home Office, with NORTHERN IRELAND counting separately. THE EXCLUSIONS ARE THE POINT. Canada's CCAC covers only CERTIFIED INSTITUTIONS — typically universities — so most private laboratories and companies are absent unless government-funded, and the CCAC sets no standardised submission method. The US counts only AWA-covered mammals, excluding mice, rats and birds; official figures near 800,000 sit against unofficial estimates of 12–24 million. INVERTEBRATES SUCH AS FRUIT FLIES AND WORMS ARE NOT PROTECTED AND NOT COUNTED ANYWHERE. And JAPAN PUBLISHES NO OFFICIAL GOVERNMENT DATA at all — the only figures come from a professional association survey to which a third of facilities did not respond. Where a country publishes nothing, an estimate is all that exists.
Visit source ↗
▸CHECKING A CLINIC’S RECORD4
African Federation of Fertility Societies
FERTILITY
The regional federation, which sets standards and runs training where no statutory regulator exists. Most African fertility care is private and unlicensed, so a professional body is often the only body holding standards. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.
Visit source ↗
ANARA — African Network and Registry for ART
FERTILITY
Collects cycle-by-cycle data from the ART centres that choose to submit it and publishes procedure counts, pregnancy and delivery rates and centre numbers by country. Reporting is voluntary and centre-led, so a country showing nothing may have clinics that have never submitted rather than no clinics. It does not license a clinic, inspect one, or take a complaint about one. One point applies to every professional register in this category: it is not a licence. A clinic missing from it may simply not have joined, and a clinic in it has met a society's conditions rather than a state's. Where a country has no statutory regulator, this is the best record available and also not a register of who is permitted to practise.
Visit source ↗
Checking a clinic where no register exists
FERTILITY
Most of the world publishes nothing clinic by clinic. Where there is no register, ask the clinic directly for its own figures, for which body licenses it, and for its last inspection — and treat a refusal as information.
ICMART and the regional ART registries — where a country has no clinic-by-clinic register
Most countries publish nothing clinic by clinic, but almost every region has a REGISTRY THAT COLLECTS THE CYCLES ANYWAY, and ICMART aggregates them into an annual WORLD REPORT. The regional bodies are worth naming because they are who to ask: ANARA for Africa (contributing countries have included Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Ivory Coast, Kenya, Libya, Mali, Mauritius, Nigeria, South Africa, Sudan, Togo, Tunisia, Uganda and Zimbabwe); ESHRE's EUROPEAN IVF MONITORING CONSORTIUM (EIM) for Europe; REDLARA for Latin America; ANZARD for Australia and New Zealand; CARTR Plus for Canada; SART for the US; JSOG and JSRM for Japan; MEFS for the Middle East; ASPIRE for Asia-Pacific. EIM collects IVF, ICSI, frozen embryo transfer, EGG DONATION, in-vitro maturation, FROZEN OOCYTE REPLACEMENT and pooled data on PREIMPLANTATION GENETIC TESTING. TWO LIMITS TO CARRY: the legal obligation on a clinic to report to its national authority VARIES WIDELY BY COUNTRY and participation changes every year, so the totals are a floor rather than a count; and ICMART is funded partly by UNRESTRICTED GRANTS FROM ABBOTT AND FERRING PHARMACEUTICALS alongside the professional societies.
Visit source ↗
▸COMPLAINTS AND DONOR REGISTRIES3
Donor Sibling Registry
FERTILITY

FERTILITY
Complaints about a clinic go to whichever body licenses it — a dedicated regulator where one exists, otherwise the health ministry. Where the clinic is private and unlicensed, consumer protection may be the only route.
Statutory donor registers and the right to know — where the law gives one
THE QUESTION HERE IS OFTEN NOT A COMPLAINT BUT ACCESS TO A RECORD, and in a minority of jurisdictions the law creates one. SWEDEN WAS FIRST, ABOLISHING ANONYMOUS SPERM DONATION IN 1985, with people born after 1 March 1985 entitled to identifying information; the UK and FINLAND have also banned anonymous gamete donation, and in AUSTRALIA anonymous donation is not possible. VICTORIA is the fullest model and worth knowing in detail because it shows what a register can do: a CENTRAL REGISTER holding identifying information on all parties to a donor procedure that resulted in a birth, and a VOLUNTARY REGISTER through which people including DONOR SIBLINGS can record their own details; donor-conceived people and their DESCENDANTS may apply at 18 for the donor's name, date of birth and donor code; DONORS MAY ALSO APPLY for information about their offspring; 2017 amendments REMOVED THE REQUIREMENT FOR DONOR CONSENT, replacing it with CONTACT PREFERENCES; donors are limited to ten recipient women; and from 1 January 2010 the fact of donor conception is recorded on the birth register, with an addendum issued to the person themselves — not to parents — from 1 January 2028. NOTE THE CHANGE: VARTA ceased operations on 31 December 2024 and the registers passed to the DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH's Donor Conception Registrar. Only three Australian states have such registers, and most of the world has none — where none exists, the Donor Sibling Registry in this box is the alternative.

WHO ICTRP — the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform
Ten country rows in this file send a reader to the ICTRP and it was not itself listed. It is a SEARCH PORTAL across the national and regional registries rather than a register in its own right: one query reaches ClinicalTrials.gov, the EU register, the Chinese, Indian, Iranian, Japanese, Korean, Cuban, Peruvian, Thai, Dutch, Brazilian, Australian-New Zealand and other primary registries at once. Two limits worth knowing: it only shows what a primary registry has published, so a trial registered nowhere is invisible here too; and records are supplied by those registries, so the detail and the update frequency vary by source. Where a country's own register is thin, unpublished or restricted, this is the way in. Searches every national registry at once, which matters because trials in China, India, Iran and Japan are often registered nationally and not in the US registry.

The WHO network of primary registries — the register that covers your region
ICTRP SEARCHES THESE; THIS PAGE NAMES THEM, which matters when you want to search in your own language or register a trial locally. Around SEVENTEEN PRIMARY REGISTRIES feed the platform: ISRCTN (the first, from 2000), the EU Clinical Trials Register, DRKS (Germany), the Netherlands NTR, ANZCTR (Australia and New Zealand), ChiCTR (China), the JAPAN REGISTRY OF CLINICAL TRIALS, CRiS (Republic of Korea), TCTR (Thailand), CTRI (India), SLCTR (Sri Lanka), IRCT (Iran), ReBec (Brazil), RPCEC (Cuba), REPEC (Peru), the LEBANESE registry (LBCTR, the most recent, from September 2019), an International Traditional Medicine registry, and PACTR. PACTR IS THE ONE TO KNOW FOR AFRICA: managed by Cochrane South Africa at the Medical Research Council, begun 2007 as the AIDS, TB and Malaria registry, widened in 2009 to all conditions, and IT IS THE ONLY AFRICAN PRIMARY REGISTRY IN THE WHO NETWORK — so a trial anywhere on the continent should be there, and South Africa additionally runs SANCTR. THE HONEST LIMITS: registry scale is wildly uneven, from a few hundred trials in Cuba to tens of thousands in the EU register; completeness of records differs sharply between registries; and ICTRP's own search interface is frequently slow or unavailable, so going direct to the regional registry is often faster.

▸WHO OVERSEES CONTAINMENT2
Where containment is not reportable
LABS
In most countries laboratory work is notified rather than licensed, notifications are not published, and there is no public complaint route. The honest first question is which body holds the notifications — ask the Cartagena focal point.
Institutional biosafety committees — the tier that exists even where there is no national register
In most countries contained laboratory work is NOTIFIED rather than licensed and no public register is created — which is why 184 of the country boxes in this file carry no national entry here. A second tier usually does exist. Under the CARTAGENA PROTOCOL, LMOs destined for CONTAINED USE fall under ARTICLE 6 and are EXEMPT FROM THE ADVANCE INFORMED AGREEMENT PROCEDURE — contained work is deliberately outside the route that generates public records — though the handling and labelling duties in Article 18 still apply and a Party MAY REQUIRE NOTIFICATION BEFORE TRANSIT. What national biosafety frameworks create instead is an INSTITUTIONAL BIOSAFETY COMMITTEE inside every organisation doing the work, usually with a named BIOSAFETY OFFICER and PRINCIPAL INVESTIGATOR, CERTIFIED BY AND REPORTING TO the national biosafety committee. Ghana's Biosafety (Management of Biotechnology) Regulations 2007 set this out explicitly, as do India's Rules 1989. THE PRACTICAL POINT: where no national register exists, the record of what a laboratory is doing sits with that institution's own biosafety committee, and the national focal point listed on the Biosafety Clearing-House is who can be asked whether one has been certified.
